title: Kola: The World’s Deepest Hole
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck explore the Kola Superdeep Borehole near Zapolyarny on the Kola Peninsula in Soviet Russia, drilled from 1970 to 1989 to about 12,262 meters, the deepest hole ever dug. They cover the American Project Mohole that preceded it, the Moho and Conrad discontinuities, the drilling problems (bit changes, rock density, deflection, pipe failure, fishing expeditions), the heat that ended the project, the water and fossil findings, the Oceanic crust holes off Costa Rica, the German KTB borehole and Lotte Gerver's recording, and a listener mail segment about MASH.
topics: Costa Rica Rift deep sea drilling

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with Simpsons references and banter about Jerry, then tease the topic of a Cold War-style race between the USSR and the United States to dig deep into the Earth.

segments.title: Project Mohole and the Moho discontinuity
segments.summary: The hosts describe the American Project Mohole, which aimed to drill through the ocean floor to the mantle, named as a joke on the Moho discontinuity, the boundary between crust and mantle named after Mohorovičić, whose seismic work identified it. The American Miscellaneous Society proposed the idea in the 1950s; drilling began off Guadalupe Island and reached just over 600 feet before funding ended in 1966. John Steinbeck documented the project.

segments.title: Start of the Kola Superdeep Borehole
segments.summary: After Project Mohole ended in 1966, the Soviets began the Kola Superdeep Borehole near Murmansk, close to the Norwegian border and the Barents Sea. It is named for the Kola Peninsula and is the deepest hole ever dug by humans.

segments.title: Hole size and current condition
segments.summary: The hosts note the hole is only about nine inches (23 cm) in diameter and is covered by a plate with rusty bolts. The marked depth is wrong because the last two digits were transposed, and the hole has shifted and caved in and is full of debris, so nothing can be dropped in.

segments.title: How deep it is, in comparisons
segments.summary: The borehole is about 7.6 miles or 12,262 meters deep, deeper than the Mariana Trench's lowest point and deeper than Mount Everest is tall, so Mount Fuji could sit atop Everest and still not reach its bottom. It is also deeper than a commercial airliner's cruising altitude.

segments.title: Original goal of reaching the mantle
segments.summary: The Soviets aimed to reach the mantle, expecting to get down to about 15 kilometers, but stopped at roughly 12 km. The hosts reference a Charlotte Wriggley article on the project in Environment and Planning D.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before returning to the show.

segments.title: Earth's layers primer
segments.summary: Josh gives a primer on Earth's layers: crust (continental and oceanic, averaging about 25 miles or 40 km), the mantle, the outer core, and the inner core, with a possible super-liquid inner core. Off-topic banter follows about the Dio tattoo.

segments.title: Depth context and the 1970 to 1989 timeline
segments.summary: Drilling began May 24, 1970, broke digging records by 1979, and reached about 4,230 feet... the hosts summarize that drilling stopped in 1989 at its deepest point and that the hole covers about 0.2 percent of the distance to Earth's center.

segments.title: Other deep holes and reasons for deep drilling
segments.summary: The hosts compare the Bingham Canyon Copper Mine in Salt Lake City and the Big Hole diamond mine in South Africa, which was dug by hand, and discuss reasons for deep drilling: minerals, fossil fuels, science, geohazards, geothermal energy, and climate history.

segments.title: Science goals: earthquakes, seismic imaging and ancient crust
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the value of deep holes for studying earthquakes and microquakes, improving predictions, and seismic imaging of Earth's interior. They note that the drilled crust is pre-Cambrian, up to about 538 million years old, and that the Soviets wanted to develop techniques for deep oil wells.

segments.title: Why rock core samples matter
segments.summary: Core samples brought to the surface are crumbly, but they still provide undisturbed views of deep crust. The hosts reflect on human curiosity as the driving reason for such holes.

segments.title: Drilling difficulties: bits, pipes and deflection
segments.summary: The hosts explain that drill bits lasted only about four hours or 30 feet before needing changes that took up to eight hours. Smooth progress until about 4.3 miles, then denser rock pushed the bit sideways, causing deviation. Steel pipe casings had trouble with pressure, leading to a branching, Christmas-tree-shaped set of holes.

segments.title: Fishing expeditions and branching shafts
segments.summary: When drill bits or casing broke or caved in, crews had to fish out debris, one of which took five years according to Wriggley. To keep moving, they started side holes, so the project is one central shaft with branches.

segments.title: The temperature problem
segments.summary: Around 12,000 feet (about 3 km) the temperature jumped unexpectedly, reaching about 356 degrees F (180 C) at roughly 7.5 miles. Heat and pressure made the rock plastic, like gelatin, and the project was stopped.

segments.title: End of the project and funding collapse
segments.summary: Work continued until about 1992 and was formally sealed in 2005, with peak staffing around 700 people. The Soviet Union's dissolution and lack of funding led to mothballing in 2008, with the last employees unpaid for six months.

segments.title: Revised temperature maps and the Conrad discontinuity
segments.summary: The findings required updated temperature maps. The Conrad discontinuity, proposed in the 1930s between upper crust granite and basalt, was disproved, and the hosts say the researchers mocked Conrad's descendants.

segments.title: Deep water and secrecy about the Soviet hole
segments.summary: The Soviets found saline water in cracks deeper than expected. Water is thought to be carried down by subducting plates, and the Soviets kept the project secret for 14 years before announcing it at a 1984 geological conference in Moscow.

segments.title: Marine fossils found deep underground
segments.summary: The most surprising finding was marine organism fossils about two billion years old at roughly 7 km (4.5 miles) down. The hosts stress these were carried down by plate tectonics and did not live at that depth.

segments.title: Future drilling toward the mantle and the Costa Rica effort
segments.summary: The hosts consider whether modern technology could reach the mantle and note that funding is the obstacle. Thin oceanic crust could make it easier. A group drilled off Costa Rica in the early 2000s, reaching about 1.25 km before funding ended.

segments.title: Pizza tangent
segments.summary: Hosts digress into a Domino's pizza tangent, with off-topic chat about pizza in Atlanta and Florida. This is not a sponsor read.

segments.title: German KTB borehole and the recording of its sound
segments.summary: The Germans drilled a deeper hole in the 1990s, reaching about 9 km (5.6 miles), with bits that withstood 260 C. Dutch artist Lotte Gerver lowered a microphone and recorded a rumbling sound that science cannot fully explain. An urban legend about hellish screams is dismissed.

segments.title: Wrap-up
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up the Kola episode and apologize for the bleaching references.

segments.title: Listener mail on MASH
segments.summary: A listener writes about the MASH episode, including the show's camp-move bug, and another listener comments that the drinking by BJ and Hawkeye was a way to pass time.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Corporate-name callout for Toledo listeners and the closing tagline.
